title: Controlled-Impedance Source Control for Grid-Connected Converters in Series-Compensated Photovoltaic Systems
abstract: Photovoltaic systems integrated with battery energy storage may exchange power with the utility grid through series-compensated networks. Their grid interfaces must support both rectifying operation for grid-to-storage charging and inverting operation for power export from photovoltaic generation or storage. However, interactions between conventional phase-locked-loop (PLL)-based control and series-compensated networks can cause subsynchronous resonance (SSR), limiting stable operation. This paper proposes a PLL-free controlled-impedance-source strategy that shapes the converter terminal characteristic to support bidirectional power exchange. The frequency-dependent impedance is analyzed to establish parameter-selection guidelines, and the steady-state operating points are derived to support voltage-loop design. Root-locus analysis incorporating current-measurement filtering, sampling, and delay effects evaluates the closed-loop stability under rectifying and inverting conditions. Controller-hardware-in-the-loop experiments compare the proposed strategy with conventional PLL-based control at different short-circuit ratios (SCRs) and series-compensation levels. The proposed controller maintains stable operation under tested conditions in which the PLL-based controller exhibits subsynchronous oscillations. Additional inverting-mode experiments show stable operation at SCR = 2.5 and a loss of stability following a transition to SCR = 2.0, consistent with the predicted stability limitation. These results demonstrate the applicability of the proposed strategy to bidirectional grid interfaces in series-compensated photovoltaic–storage systems within the investigated operating range.

title: Agentic AI for intelligent battery management systems: From diagnosis to autonomous control
abstract: Battery management systems (BMSs) are evolving from threshold-based supervisory units and isolated predictive modules toward intelligent, closed-loop decision architectures capable of diagnosis, prognosis, optimization, and autonomous control. This review examines how agentic artificial intelligence extends conventional AI-enabled BMS research by integrating state awareness, risk-informed reasoning, goal-driven planning, and safety-constrained action across cell-, pack-, and system-level operations. Rather than merely cataloguing prior studies, the review compares major groups of works spanning data-driven state estimation, degradation modeling, reinforcement learning-based control, hybrid physics-informed methods, digital twins, and emerging multi-agent strategies, highlighting their respective strengths, operational assumptions, scalability limits, interpretability, and deployment readiness. The analysis shows that prediction-oriented approaches remain dominant, while comparatively fewer studies achieve robust closed-loop autonomy under uncertainty, aging, thermal coupling, and heterogeneous usage conditions. To address this gap, the paper proposes the Agentic Battery Management Stack (A-BMS), a six-layer framework linking multimodal sensing, health inference, predictive risk assessment, decision intelligence, autonomous control execution, and human oversight. The review concludes by identifying key barriers and research priorities for trustworthy, adaptive, and certifiable autonomous battery management.

title: Simultaneous determination of reaction and diffusion kinetics in lithium-ion batteries using symmetric current pulse
abstract: Accurate electrochemical parameterisation of lithium-ion batteries is essential for physics-based modelling, electrode design, and safety assessment, yet conventional approaches such as galvanostatic intermittent titration (GITT) for diffusion and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) for reaction kinetics are typically performed separately and require several weeks to generate comprehensive temperature and state of charge (SoC) resolved datasets. Here, a symmetric current pulse (SCP) methodology is introduced that determines both reaction and diffusion kinetics within a single integrated workflow. A symmetric charge-discharge pulse sequence at each SoC point preserves the open-circuit voltage and minimises SoC drift, enabling the thermodynamically consistent extraction of reaction kinetics (charge-transfer resistance, exchange current density, electrode reaction rate) and diffusion kinetics (lithium diffusion coefficient) directly from transient voltage responses. Subsequent EIS measurements at the same SoC provide independent validation of the reaction kinetics via distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis. Applied to NMC622//Li and graphite//Li half-cells over 20–100 % SoC and 10–45 °C, the methodology yields parameter maps in strong agreement with conventional GITT and EIS, while reducing total characterisation time from several weeks to approximately four days. The resulting temperature- and SoC-dependent kinetic maps reveal high-resistance and diffusion-limited operating regimes characterised by severe polarisation and transport limitations that may be associated with increased lithium-plating susceptibility. This provides a practical and fast route to safety-informed cell design and physics-based model parameterisation applicable across electrode chemistries and formats for energy storage.
title_zh: Simultaneous determination of reaction and diffusion kinetics in lithium-ion batteries using symmetric current pulse
